What is the essential teaching in 'For the Welfare of Many'?

In 'For the Welfare of Many', the teaching opens with this observation: *"In the hour before dawn on Wednesday, 19th October 1994, our esteemed Founding-President and Patron, Venerable Nyanaponika Mahathera, passed away peacefully at his residence, the Forest Hermitage in the Udawattakele Reserve, Kandy."* The central invitation is to turn one's investigation inward — to verify the Dhamma not as a set of beliefs, but as directly observable reality in one's own body, speech, and mind. As the text teaches, the Dhamma is *akāliko* — ever-present — and *opanayiko* — leading inward — available to be known (*paccattaṁ*) by each practitioner for themselves. There is no need to search elsewhere; the truth is already here.

This text mentions stress (dukkha). Can you explain its role in practice?

In this text, dukkha appears in this context: *"His interpretations of the Dhamma always flowed from a clear personal discernment of its innermost essence — the Four Noble Truths and the three characteristics — and were built upon a solid respect f"* Understanding stress (dukkha) — the first noble truth is not merely conceptual — it is meant to be verified directly. The Dhamma is *ehipassiko*: 'come and see for yourself.' Bring the quality described by dukkha into direct investigation: where is it present in your current experience? When seen clearly, each of these Pāli terms dissolves from abstract concept into living reality.
